title: Third-Party Scripts and Supply Chain
summary: Every third-party tag runs with exactly your privileges, so their compromise is your breach. Learn Subresource Integrity, iframe sandboxing, and how CSP limits the blast radius when a vendor is owned.

slides.markdown:
A typical production page loads code from between five and twenty organisations: analytics, error tracking, session replay, A/B testing, chat, ads, consent management, a payment SDK, a font host.

Every one of those scripts runs **in your origin, with your privileges**. There is no permission model, no sandbox, and no partial trust. A vendor's script can read your DOM, read anything in `localStorage`, call your API with the user's cookies attached, and rewrite your checkout form — because to the browser it is indistinguishable from code your team wrote.

So your security posture is the *union* of every vendor's security posture, plus their build systems, plus their npm dependencies, plus whoever has commit access at each of them. That's the supply chain.

You cannot audit all of it. What you can do is **contain it**: pin what you can with Subresource Integrity, isolate what you can in a sandboxed iframe, and constrain what any of it can reach with CSP — so that a vendor compromise is an incident rather than a breach.

The browser's unit of trust is the **origin**, not the file. A script's privileges come from the document that loaded it, not from where it was fetched — so `<script src="https://vendor.example/a.js">` on your page executes with your page's authority, exactly as `/app.js` does.

Concretely, any third-party script on your page can:

- Read and modify the entire DOM, including form fields as the user types them.
- Read `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, and any non-`HttpOnly` cookie.
- Call your API with the session cookie attached automatically, or read a bearer token from wherever your app keeps it.
- Register event listeners on your forms, or replace your submit handler.
- Load further scripts, which inherit the same privileges.
- Install a service worker, gaining persistence across sessions.

This is why "we only use reputable vendors" is a procurement statement, not a security control. The question isn't whether the vendor is trustworthy today — it's what happens on the day their CDN, their build pipeline, or one of their transitive npm dependencies is compromised, and whether that becomes your incident or your breach.

See [xss-fundamentals](xss-fundamentals) for the same capability set arriving by injection. The difference is that here you invited it.

slides.subTitle: Three shapes, all real
slides.markdown:
Three well-documented incidents, each a different link in the chain. The point is the shape, not the detail.

**The loaded script itself is altered — Magecart.** In the 2018 British Airways breach, a small amount of modified JavaScript on the payment page skimmed card details from roughly 380,000 transactions over about two weeks. The ICO's initial penalty announcement was £183m, later settled at £20m. Nothing about the site was "hacked" in the way people picture: a script that was supposed to be there was doing something extra. The same pattern hit Ticketmaster via a chat widget vendor.

**A dependency in your own build — `event-stream`.** In 2018 a widely-used npm package was handed to a new maintainer who added a malicious transitive dependency targeting a specific cryptocurrency wallet. It reached millions of weekly downloads before discovery. Nothing on your CDN changed; the poison shipped inside your own bundle.

**A whole domain changing hands — Polyfill.io.** In 2024 the domain behind a script embedded on a very large number of sites was acquired, after which it began serving conditionally malicious code. Sites that had pasted the tag years earlier were affected without doing anything at all.

The generalisable lesson: **the compromise usually happens somewhere you have no visibility, and the first signal is behavioural.** Design for detection and containment, not for prevention.

slides.subTitle: Pinning a script to a hash
slides.markdown:
**SRI** lets you state the exact bytes you expect. The browser fetches the file, hashes it, and refuses to execute it if the hash doesn't match.

```html
<script
  src="https://cdn.example.com/lib@3.2.1/lib.min.js"
  integrity="sha384-oqVuAfXRKap7fdgcCY5uykM6+R9GqQ8K/uxy9rx7HNQlGYl1kPzQho1wx4JwY8wC"
  crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
```

Generate the hash from the file you reviewed:

```bash
curl -s https://cdn.example.com/lib@3.2.1/lib.min.js \
  | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary \
  | openssl base64 -A
```

Four details that decide whether it works:

- **`crossorigin="anonymous"` is mandatory** for cross-origin resources. Without it the response is opaque, the browser can't verify it, and the script is blocked — the most common reason SRI "breaks the site."
- **`sha384` is the usual choice**; `sha256` and `sha512` are also valid, and you may list several space-separated hashes so one tag covers a planned version bump.
- **Pin an immutable, versioned URL.** SRI on a `@latest` URL guarantees breakage the moment the vendor publishes.
- **A mismatch is a hard block, not a warning.** That's the desired behaviour, and it means a vendor changing a file silently takes your feature offline — which is a real availability trade you should make deliberately.

slides.sectionTitle: SRI at the moment of compromise
slides.markdown:
Follow one page load on the day the CDN is serving altered code.

1. The browser parses your page and finds a script tag with `src`, `integrity`, and `crossorigin`.
2. It fetches the file. What comes back is the vendor's library **plus** extra code — an attacker's edit, invisible in the URL and identical in size order.
3. Before executing anything, the browser hashes the received bytes and compares against the `integrity` value.
4. They differ. The browser **refuses to execute the script**, logs an integrity error to the console, and fires an `error` event on the element.
5. Your page continues without that feature. Nothing from the altered file ran — not one line, because verification happens before parsing.

Two consequences worth holding onto. The failure is **fail-closed**, so a compromised vendor degrades your feature rather than breaching your users. And it is **observable**: an `onerror` handler on the tag, or a CSP report endpoint, turns a silent supply-chain attack into an alert — often before the vendor's own status page mentions anything.

![Five-stage pipeline showing a script tag with an integrity attribute, a compromised CDN response, a hash mismatch, and the script refused before parsing](assets/sri-hash-mismatch-pipeline.svg)

assets.alt: Five-stage pipeline showing a script tag with an integrity attribute, a compromised CDN response, a hash mismatch, and the script refused before parsing

slides.markdown:
SRI is genuinely useful and covers a narrower slice than people assume. Knowing the gaps is the senior half of this topic.

- **It only covers resources you reference by tag.** A script that loads more scripts at runtime — which is what tag managers, ad stacks and most analytics loaders do by design — is unpinned from the second file onward.
- **It's incompatible with intentionally dynamic endpoints.** Services that tailor their response per browser change bytes per request, so no fixed hash exists. That is exactly the Polyfill.io shape, and it's why such services can't be pinned.
- **It doesn't protect your build.** A malicious npm dependency is compiled into your own bundle, which you then hash yourself. SRI faithfully verifies the compromised file.
- **It says nothing about behaviour.** A vendor can publish a new, correctly-hashed version that legitimately does something you'd object to. SRI checks identity, not intent.
- **It has an availability cost.** Fail-closed means a vendor's routine minifier change takes your widget offline until someone updates the hash. Teams that hit this twice often remove SRI rather than automate the update — which is the real-world failure mode.

The conclusion isn't to skip SRI. It's that SRI answers "is this the file I reviewed?" and you still need CSP to answer "what can it reach?" and sandboxing to answer "what can it touch?"

slides.subTitle: The only real isolation boundary in the browser
slides.markdown:
If a script must run but doesn't need your DOM, put it in a **separate origin inside a sandboxed iframe**. That is the one place the browser gives you a genuine privilege boundary rather than a policy.

```html
<iframe src="https://widget-sandbox.example.net/chat"
        sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"
        referrerpolicy="no-referrer"></iframe>
```

The `sandbox` attribute is **deny-by-default**: with no tokens the frame gets a unique opaque origin, no script execution, no forms, no top-level navigation, no popups, no storage access. Each token adds one capability back:

- `allow-scripts` — run JS, usually required.
- `allow-forms`, `allow-popups`, `allow-modals` — grant only if the widget needs them.
- `allow-top-navigation` — almost never grant this; it's what lets a frame redirect the whole page.
- **`allow-same-origin` — the one that matters.** Combined with `allow-scripts` on a frame you host from *your own* origin, it lets the frame reach out and remove its own sandbox attribute. Never pair those two for content you don't control; host the frame on a different origin.

The frame communicates with your page over `postMessage` only, so you get an explicit, reviewable API surface instead of blanket DOM access — and you must validate `event.origin` on every message, or you've built a new hole.

The cost is real: many vendors don't support being framed, and the integration work is on you.

slides.subTitle: Different questions, different answers
slides.markdown:
| | Subresource Integrity | CSP allowlist / nonces | `<iframe sandbox>` on another origin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Question it answers | is this the exact file I reviewed? | which sources may run, and where may they send data? | what can this code touch at all? |
| Stops an altered CDN response | **yes** | no — the host is still allowed | contained to the frame |
| Stops a legitimately-published malicious update | no | no | yes, mostly |
| Stops exfiltration to an attacker's server | no | **yes**, via `connect-src` | yes, the frame has its own policy |
| Covers scripts loaded by the script | no | partly, via `'strict-dynamic'` | yes |
| Protects against a poisoned npm dependency | no | only the exfiltration step | no, if it's in your own bundle |
| Integration cost | low | medium, plus rollout | high, and vendor support varies |

They compose, and the composition is the point: **SRI pins identity, CSP constrains reach, the sandbox removes access.** A vendor compromise that gets past SRI — because they published a real update — still has to exfiltrate through a `connect-src` that names only hosts you approved.

If you can only do one thing, do the CSP `connect-src`. Stolen data has to leave the browser somehow, and that directive is the chokepoint every variant of this attack must pass through. Details in [content-security-policy](content-security-policy).

slides.sectionTitle: The half of the supply chain in your build
slides.markdown:
Runtime tags get the attention; the larger surface is usually `node_modules`. A mid-sized frontend app routinely resolves over a thousand transitive packages, most of which no one on the team has read a line of.

Controls that pay for themselves:

- **Commit the lockfile and install with `npm ci`.** A build that resolves fresh versions can pull a package published minutes ago. Lockfiles also make a compromise reproducible and auditable after the fact.
- **Delay adoption of new versions.** Most malicious packages are discovered within hours to days, so a cooldown window before a version becomes installable removes most of the exposure at near-zero cost.
- **Ignore install scripts by default.** `npm ci --ignore-scripts` blocks the lifecycle hooks that malicious packages most often use. Allowlist the few genuine ones.
- **Audit and monitor**, with `npm audit` or a scanner in CI, understanding that these find *known* vulnerabilities, not new attacks.
- **Watch for the human factors** that preceded real incidents: a maintainer handover on a package with millions of downloads, a dependency with one maintainer and no recent activity, a typosquatted name one character off a popular package.
- **Prefer fewer dependencies.** Every package added is a permanent grant of code execution in your build and your users' browsers.

And note what SRI cannot do here: a malicious dependency is compiled into your own bundle, which you hash yourself, so the integrity check passes perfectly.

slides.subTitle: The ungoverned tag
slides.markdown:
The realistic version of this risk is not a sophisticated attack. It's a pasted snippet.

A campaign needs a pixel. Someone with tag-manager access adds it on a Friday. No engineer reviews it, no `integrity` attribute exists because the vendor serves a versionless URL, and no one records who owns it. Two years later nobody in the company knows what it does, and the vendor may not even be a customer relationship anymore.

Why this is the dominant failure mode:

- **A tag manager is a remote code execution channel by design.** Anyone with container access can push arbitrary JavaScript to production, bypassing code review, CI, and your release process entirely. It is usually the least-governed deploy path a company has.
- **The tag loads more tags.** One container often pulls in a dozen further vendors, none of which appear in any inventory.
- **Nobody removes anything.** Tags accumulate; campaigns end and the code stays.

What actually works, in order of effort:

1. **Inventory.** A recurring crawl of production listing every script origin loaded. Most teams are surprised by the result the first time.
2. **An owner per tag**, with a review date. No owner means it gets removed.
3. **CSP as the enforcement point**, so adding a genuinely new vendor requires a policy change that goes through engineering — this converts a social process into a technical gate without blocking marketing's day-to-day work.
4. **Sandbox or server-side tagging** for anything that doesn't need your DOM.

You will not prevent every vendor compromise, so the metric that matters is **time to detect**. British Airways ran for roughly two weeks; the theoretical minimum with the right signals is minutes.

Signals that actually fire:

- **CSP violation reports.** A script suddenly attempting a `connect-src` to a host that isn't on your list is close to a definitive signal, and it arrives from real user traffic rather than from a scanner. This is the strongest single reason to keep a report endpoint running permanently in production.
- **SRI failures.** An `onerror` handler on pinned tags, reported to your monitoring, tells you a vendor's bytes changed — whether that's an attack or a careless deploy.
- **Synthetic monitoring on sensitive pages.** A headless browser loading checkout on a schedule and diffing the set of network destinations and script origins against a baseline catches what CSP would have allowed.
- **Third-party script inventory drift.** An unexpected new origin appearing is worth an alert on its own.
- **Client-side error rate by vendor.** Injected code frequently produces new exception signatures before anyone notices anything else.

And the response plan is worth having written down *before* you need it: how do you remove a vendor's script from production **in minutes**? If the answer involves a full release cycle, that's the gap to fix — a kill switch behind a feature flag or an edge rule is the difference between a two-hour incident and a two-week one.

How to answer "a vendor script got compromised — what limited the damage?" The honest answer is a stack of partial controls, roughly by value:

1. **A tight CSP `connect-src`.** Exfiltration has to leave the browser somewhere. This is the chokepoint every variant passes through, and the one that also generates the alert.
2. **Keeping the vendor off your most sensitive pages entirely.** No third-party script on checkout, login, or account settings is the cheapest, strongest control available, and it's an architectural decision rather than a technology.
3. **Sandboxed iframes on a separate origin** for anything that doesn't need your DOM. This is real isolation rather than policy.
4. **`HttpOnly` cookies and no bearer token in `localStorage`**, so there's nothing readable to take — see [secure-storage-and-tokens](secure-storage-and-tokens).
5. **SRI on everything with a stable versioned URL**, plus automated hash updates so it doesn't get removed out of frustration.
6. **Build-side hygiene** — lockfiles, `npm ci`, `--ignore-scripts`, a version cooldown.
7. **Detection and a rehearsed kill switch**, because containment failing quietly for two weeks is the actual worst case.

The framing that reads as senior: you cannot make third-party code trustworthy, so **stop trying to and start bounding it**. Every control above is about what a compromised vendor can reach, not about whether they get compromised.
